3. What is this, in plain words

A cache is a short-term memory. Instead of asking the database "is this workspace suspended?" on every request, the app remembers the answer for a few seconds. A hit means the memory had the answer. A miss means the app had to ask the source. An error means the memory itself broke (for example Redis was down) and the app asked the source anyway.

Analogy: a shop assistant who keeps the day's prices on a sticky note. If the note is right most of the time, the shop is fast. If the note is lost or wrong, every customer waits while the assistant walks to the back office. Before this task, nobody could see how often the note was right. Now there is a tally mark for each outcome, and an alarm when the tally looks bad.

Glossary
Counter: a number that only goes up; Prometheus reads it every 15 s.
Label: a tag on a number, here only cache="rbac_grants". A label with a user id would create one series per user and break the monitoring system, so it is forbidden.
Series: one counter with one set of labels.
Hit ratio: hits divided by (hits plus misses).
Recording rule / alert rule: a saved Prometheus query / a query that raises a warning.
Register: docs/performance/cache/register.json, the list of all 69 caches from task #64.
promtool: Prometheus's own rule checker and tester.

4. How we tested

  1. Instrument. One helper, cacheMetrics('name'), in packages/observability. It exposes crm_cache_hits_total, crm_cache_misses_total, crm_cache_errors_total and crm_cache_entries on the existing metrics listener (the one that already serves event-loop and queue series). Rule: an error is counted as an error and also as a miss, because the request went to the source.
  2. Wire the helper at each hit/miss point named in the register (52 caches, 53 metric names).
  3. Ratchet. A test reads the source and the register and fails if a cache has neither a counter call nor a written exemption, if a counter name is computed instead of a literal, or if the alert's cache list drifts from the register. Each rule was also run on deliberately bad input and fails there.
  4. Behaviour tests on real classes: one count per lookup (fake Redis, and a private-scope real Redis for the RBAC Lua path), a throwing metrics sink, 10,000 workspaces, ratio workloads.
  5. Overhead: the same benchmark file run alternately (5 rounds) on this branch and on its merge-base with origin/main.
  6. Rules checked and unit-tested with promtool v2.55.0 (docker image, a throwaway container).

7. Rollout and rollback

Metrics only; no behaviour changes in the request path. Steps: deploy the API and worker (counters appear at /metrics); mount cache-hit-rate.rules.yml (already added to prometheus.yml and the Hostinger observability compose file) and reload Prometheus; watch for two weeks; tune thresholds. Rollback: remove the rules file from rule_files and reload; the counters themselves cost about 17 ns per call and can stay.

8. What this does NOT prove

  • It does not show any production hit ratio. Only synthetic and fake-Redis workloads were run.
  • The alert thresholds are guesses; they have been tested to fire and not fire on synthetic data, not on real traffic.
  • Alerts were not run in a live Prometheus with Alertmanager routing; only promtool unit tests.
  • The overhead numbers come from one laptop, fake Redis and in-process caches. A real network round trip is thousands of times larger than 17 ns, so the share is lower in production, but this was not measured there.
  • Six browser/Next caches are not counted at all (F4). The web server's /metrics was not scraped; no web file changed.
  • Job queues ("async paths") were not re-tested here.
  • Real Redis was exercised only for the RBAC Lua path (shared dev Redis, db 13, random workspace ids, own keys removed). Other Redis classes ran against the fake.
  • Counters are per process and reset on restart; Prometheus rate() handles resets but the ratio is not per workspace by design.
  • The merged result was tested with the unit suite only; no integration or e2e suite was run (they need Docker databases).
